title: The Echo Voyage

topics.value_lesson: Listening carefully can show us things that looking cannot

spine: We travel from a bat cave to the deep ocean floor, following sound as it reveals what eyes cannot see.

segments.text:
"Quick," says Pip. "They're waking up."

We are standing at the mouth of a limestone cave, and the dusk is coming down soft and grey around us. Pip is a bat researcher, which means she spends her evenings listening to sounds most people never hear. She has a microphone in one hand and a little speaker in the other, and she is grinning like someone who knows a secret.

"Look up," she whispers.

She clicks on a red torch and points it at the cave ceiling. The light is dim and rosy, and it does not bother the bats. Hundreds of them hang upside down up there, folded into their wings like little parcels. Some of them are starting to wiggle.

"They sleep all day," Pip says. "And when it gets dark, they fly out to catch moths and mosquitoes. But here is the amazing part. They do it in complete darkness. They see with sound."

We stare at her. "With sound?" we ask.

"With sound." She bounces on her toes. "It's called echolocation. A bat shouts, and the shout bounces off a moth, and the echo comes back and tells the bat exactly where that moth is. The shouts are too high for our ears. That highness is called frequency. Bat calls are such high frequency that we cannot hear them at all."

Then she lifts the microphone. "But this can."

A bat drops from the ceiling and swoops past us into the night. Pip presses a button, and her speaker plays the bat's shout slowed right down, so our ears can catch it.

"Chip! Chip-chip!"

It sounds like a tiny, speedy bird. Pip laughs. "That's him saying, where's dinner? Come on. Let's go listen properly."

"The cave it is," says Pip. "Stay close."

We follow her in, and the dark wraps around us like a blanket. Pip's red torch makes the stalactites glow dim and rosy above our heads. They hang down like stone icicles, slow-growing and patient.

"Now," Pip whispers, "watch this."

She lifts her microphone. All around us, the cave fills with a sound like soft rain on leaves. It is the flutter of hundreds of wings. We cannot see the bats, but we can hear them everywhere.

"Listen to this," Pip says. She presses a button, and her speaker plays a bat's shout slowed down. "Chip! Chip-chip-chip!" Then, a moment later, a fainter echo: "chip-chip."

"That echo tells the bat everything," Pip says. Her voice is quick and chirpy, like the bats themselves. "How far away the wall is. Whether that flutter is a moth or a mosquito. A bat can catch an echo from something as thin as a human hair."

We stand very still. The air moves with wings we cannot see. A bat swoops close, and we feel the tiny wind of it on our cheeks.

"Their ears," Pip whispers, "are like satellite dishes. They catch sounds we cannot even imagine."

We close our eyes. The cave is full of invisible music, and for a moment, we almost see it too.

"To the bay!" says Pip. "Quick, before they go!"

We hurry down the path to a quiet cove where the water is grey and still. A woman in a yellow jacket is waiting by a small boat. This is Dr. Marina. She has a microphone on a long pole, and she lowers it gently into the dusk-dark water.

"Listen," she says.

At first, there is only the soft lap of waves. Then, from the speaker, comes a sound like a creaky door. "Click-click-click." Then a whistle, long and sliding, like a flute.

"Dolphins," Dr. Marina says. "They see with sound too. They send out clicks, and the echoes come back and paint a picture in their minds."

We watch the water. It is too murky to see anything below the surface. But the dolphins know exactly where everything is.

A silver shape leaps. Then another. Dr. Marina points. "That one just found a fish. Watch."

A dolphin surfaces, ignores a grey rock, and dives after something we cannot see. A moment later, it comes up with a silver flash in its mouth.

"The rock gives one echo," Dr. Marina says. "The fish gives another. The dolphin knows the difference."

We listen to the clicks and whistles, and the dark water seems full of secrets.

Pip listens to what we found, and her eyes go wide. "That settles it," she says. "You have to see this."

She hurries us down to the harbour, where a research ship floats dark and quiet on the night water. We climb aboard, and the deck hums under our feet.

Inside, the cabin is dim. One screen glows green, like a little patch of pond weed lit from below. A technician named Marisol sits in front of it, and she waves us over without taking her eyes off the light.

"Pip says you were out listening," Marisol says. "What did you find?"

We tell her, and she grins. "Then you're ready for this. Watch."

She taps a key. From somewhere under the ship, a sound goes down into the black water.

Ping.

We wait. The green screen holds still.

Ping.

"That's sonar," Marisol says. "The ship shouts, just like a bat. The shout travels down, hits the ocean floor, and the echo comes back up. The screen listens, and it draws what the echo saw."

And it does. A bright line creeps across the green, bending and rising. It draws a hill. Then a valley. Then something tall, with a peak like a sleeping giant's shoulder.

"Down there, sunlight never reaches," Marisol says softly. "Not ever. But sound doesn't need light. Sound sees in the dark."

The peak keeps growing on the screen. Pip leans in so close her nose nearly touches the glass.

"That mountain," she whispers, "isn't on any map. Nobody has named it. Nobody even knew it was there."

We stare at the glowing green shape, a whole mountain drawn by a shout and its echo, rising out of water that has never once seen the sun.

Ping. The line moves on. The mountain stays.

"In we go," says Pip, and we climb down into {submarine_name}. It is snug inside, all round walls and little lights. Pip buckles in beside us, and her knee bounces against ours. The hatch shuts with a soft thunk.

Down we slide, into water black as the inside of a pocket. Out the window there is nothing. Nothing at all. Then the pilot taps a key.

Ping.

On the screen, the canyon wall blooms green, close enough to touch. Ping. A ledge. Ping. A crack so deep the line just falls and falls.

"The canyon is deeper than any mountain is tall," the pilot says. "And we are driving through it with our eyes closed. The pings are our eyes now."

She steers by the glowing map, slow and careful, the way you walk across a dark bedroom with your arms out. Ping. The wall swings away. Ping. Open water.

Then the screen draws something that is not rock. Straight lines. A square edge. Things the sea does not make.

"Shipwreck," the pilot breathes. "Three hundred years down here in the dark. Nobody has seen it since the day it sank."

We hold very still. The wreck sits on the green screen, drawn by sound, sleeping where it has always slept.

On the way up, Pip presses something small and cold into our hands. A shell, pale as porridge, from the canyon floor. "Found it on an earlier dive," she says. "Keep it."

When we surface, the stars are out. We hold the shell to our ear, and it hums, soft and steady, like a far-off sea remembering itself.

"That's your echo now," Pip says. "It goes where light can't. And it comes back."

"Best seats in the house," says Marisol, and she pulls up chairs beside the glowing screen. The ship hums under us, sailing slow over water black as the space between stars.

Ping.

We watch the line crawl across the green. Ping. Each shout takes ages to come back, because the trench below is so deep the sound has a long, long way to fall.

"Every ping is the ship asking a question," Marisol says. "And the dark answers. We just have to wait for it."

So we wait, all four of us, leaning toward the light. Pip's chin rests on our shoulder. The line bends, dips, and then shoots up into a peak with a crater at the top, like a bowl.

"That," Marisol whispers, "is a volcano. An underwater one, sleeping at the bottom of the sea."

Ping. The line moves on, and draws something strange. Straight edges. A mast. The sea does not make straight edges.

"A shipwreck," Pip breathes. "Ghost of the trench."

All night the map grows, line by glowing line, a whole hidden world drawn by shouts and echoes. We name the mountain together, the four of us, arguing happily, and Marisol types the name in so it stays.

At dawn the sky turns the colour of peach jam, and Marisol presses a button. A printer whirs. Out comes our map, the mountain and the volcano and the wreck, in green on white.

"A picture drawn by sound," she says, and rolls it up for us to carry home.

We hold it tight on the deck, in the new light. "Nobody else has this," says Pip. "Nobody else has ever heard this mountain."

"We have," we say. And we unroll it one more time, just to look.
